rule_en: Use the verb be to say who people are, where they are from and how they feel. Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) always come before the verb. In everyday English we usually use contractions: I'm, you're, he's.
structure: I + am / he, she, it + is / we, you, they + are
examples_en: I'm Karim and I'm from Tajikistan.
She's a new student in our class.
We're very happy today.
They're from Canada.
tip: Remember: every English sentence needs a subject — say 'It is cold', not 'Is cold'.

rule_en: Make be negative with not: I'm not, he isn't, they aren't. Make questions by putting be before the subject: Are you...? Is she...? Answer with short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.
structure: negative: subject + be + not; question: Be + subject...?
examples_en: I'm not from Russia — I'm from Uzbekistan.
He isn't at home now.
Are you tired? — No, I'm not.
Is this seat free? — Yes, it is.
tip: In short positive answers don't use contractions: say 'Yes, I am', not 'Yes, I'm'.

rule_en: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) show who something belongs to. They come before a noun and never change for plural: my book, my books.
examples_en: My email address is on this card.
What's your surname?
Her phone number is easy to remember.
Their teacher is from London.
tip: Don't confuse its (possessive) and it's (= it is).

rule_en: Most nouns add -s in the plural: key → keys. Nouns ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x add -es: watch → watches. Consonant + y changes to -ies: city → cities. Some plurals are irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people.
examples_en: There are two windows in my room.
I need three boxes for these books.
The children are in the garden.
Most people here speak two languages.
tip: Learn irregular plurals by heart — they are very common words.

rule_en: Adjectives describe nouns. They go before the noun or after be, and they never change for plural: a black cat, black cats. Modifiers very, really and quite make an adjective stronger or weaker and go before it.
examples_en: It's a really interesting film.
These shoes are quite expensive.
My city is very old and beautiful.
He drives an expensive German car.
tip: Quite is weaker than very: quite good < very good < really good.

rule_en: Use the imperative (base verb) to give instructions and orders: Sit down. Open the window. The negative is Don't + verb: Don't worry. Use Let's + verb to make a suggestion for you and other people: Let's go home.
examples_en: Turn off your phone, please.
Don't be nervous — it's only a test.
Let's have a break.
Slow down! You walk too fast.
tip: Add 'please' to sound polite: 'Close the door, please.'

rule_en: Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts. With I/you/we/they use the base verb; with he/she/it add -s. The negative is don't / doesn't + base verb.
examples_en: I cook dinner every evening.
My father works in a bank.
We don't watch TV in the morning.
She doesn't drink coffee.
tip: After doesn't the verb loses its -s: 'She doesn't work', not 'She doesn't works'.

rule_en: Make present simple questions with do / does + subject + base verb: Do you work? Does she work? Use do with I/you/we/they and does with he/she/it. The main verb never takes -s in questions.
examples_en: Do you like your job?
Does he travel a lot?
Where do they have lunch?
What time does the shop open?
tip: Answer with do/does, not the main verb: 'Yes, I do', not 'Yes, I like'.

topic: word order in questions; question words
rule_en: English questions follow a fixed order: (Question word) + auxiliary + subject + verb. Common question words: What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, How much, How many, What kind of.
examples_en: Why do you get up so early?
How many brothers does she have?
What kind of music do they play?
When does the lesson finish?
tip: Remember ASI: Auxiliary before Subject In questions.

rule_en: Add 's to a person to show possession: Anna's bag. For regular plurals add only an apostrophe: my parents' house. Ask about possession with Whose: Whose phone is this?
examples_en: This is my brother's room.
Whose keys are these? — They're Omar's.
My grandparents' photos are very old.
Karim's wife works in a hospital.
tip: 'Whose' asks about the owner; 'Who's' means 'Who is' — they sound the same!

topic: prepositions of time (at, in, on) and place (at, in, to)
rule_en: Time: at + clock time (at six), on + day or date (on Monday), in + month, season, year (in July). Place: in + city or country (in Dushanbe), at + a point or place (at work, at home), to + movement (go to school).
examples_en: I get up at half past six.
We have English on Tuesdays.
She was born in 1998.
He goes to the gym after work.
tip: Say 'at night' but 'in the morning / afternoon / evening'.

topic: position of adverbs and expressions of frequency
rule_en: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never) go before the main verb but after be. Longer expressions (every day, twice a week, once a month) usually go at the end of the sentence.
structure: subject + adverb + verb / be + adverb; expression at the end
examples_en: I usually have lunch at one.
She is never late for work.
They visit their grandmother every Sunday.
We go to the cinema twice a month.
tip: 'Never' and 'hardly ever' are already negative — don't add 'not'.

rule_en: Use can + base verb to talk about ability (I can swim) and permission (You can park here). The negative is can't (cannot). Can is the same for all persons and never takes -s or 'to'.
examples_en: She can play the guitar really well.
I can't come to the meeting tomorrow.
You can buy a newspaper at the station.
Can we sit here? — Yes, of course.
tip: Stress: in positive sentences 'can' is weak /kən/; 'can't' is strong /kɑːnt/.

rule_en: Use the present continuous (be + verb-ing) for actions happening now or around now: I'm reading. She's making noise. Spelling: make → making, sit → sitting, study → studying.
examples_en: The neighbours are playing loud music.
I'm looking for my keys.
She's talking on the phone right now.
We're waiting for the bus.
tip: Use time markers now, right now, at the moment with the present continuous.

rule_en: Present simple = habits, routines, facts (I work every day). Present continuous = actions now or temporary situations (I'm working today from home). Some verbs (like, want, know, need) are not normally used in the continuous.
structure: habit → present simple; now/temporary → present continuous
examples_en: It usually rains a lot in spring.
Take an umbrella — it's raining.
She works in a school, but this week she's working from home.
I want a cup of tea.
tip: State verbs like 'want, like, know, need' stay in the present simple.

rule_en: Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) replace a noun after a verb or preposition: I know him. Listen to me. Don't use the subject pronoun in this position.
examples_en: I love this story — read it again!
She calls her mother and talks to her every day.
Our teacher gives us a lot of homework.
Do you know them? — Yes, they're my neighbours.
tip: Pairs to remember: I→me, he→him, she→her, we→us, they→them.

rule_en: After like, love, hate and enjoy we use verb + -ing: I like dancing. For dates use ordinal numbers: the first, the second, the third, the fourth... We write '5 May' but say 'the fifth of May'.
structure: like/love/hate/enjoy + verb-ing; the + ordinal + of + month
examples_en: I love getting presents.
He hates waiting in queues.
Her birthday is on the third of June.
New Year is on the first of January.
tip: Ordinals to remember: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 5th fifth, 12th twelfth, 20th twentieth.

rule_en: Use be (am/is/are) with nouns, adjectives and -ing forms: She's a singer. Are you tired? Use do/does with other verbs in questions and negatives: Do you sing? He doesn't play. Don't mix them.
examples_en: Are you a musician? — Yes, I am.
Do you play in a band? — No, I don't.
She isn't listening to music now.
He doesn't like jazz.
tip: If the sentence has another main verb, use do/does; if not, use be.
